1.pericope_label: A man of Levi takes a daughter of Levi, who hides her goodly son three months and then lays him in an ark of bulrushes among the flags

schools.summary: John Gill says the man was Amram, the son of Kohath and grandson of Levi. The son born was not her first child, nor indeed her first son, Gill says, for she had both Aaron and Miriam before this; and he reports that the Jews say Moses was born in the thirty-seventh year after the death of Levi, in the year of the world two thousand three hundred and sixty-five, on a Wednesday, the seventh of the month Adar, at the third hour of the day, though some say it was on the twenty-fourth of Nisan, while according to Bishop Ussher he was born forty-one years after the death of Levi, in the year of the world two thousand four hundred and thirty-three, and in the year before Christ one thousand five hundred and seventy-one. She could no longer hide him because of her neighbours, who might hear the crying of the child, or because of the diligent search made by Pharaoh's officers, which some think was made every three months, Gill says; and the Jews have a notion that his mother was delivered of him at six months' end, so that when the other three months were up, which women usually go with child, she could hide him no longer, a birth being then expected and likely to be inquired after. His sister was Miriam, as the Targum of Jonathan expresses it, Gill says, who is supposed to be about ten or twelve years of age, though others say seven: she was placed by her parents, or placed herself by their instruction, at some distance from the place where the ark was, that she might not be observed and be thought to belong to it, and yet so near as to observe what became of it, which was the intent of her standing there. John Calvin says he has preferred rendering the verb in the pluperfect tense to prevent all ambiguity, for unless we say that Miriam and Aaron were the children of another mother it would not be probable that this marriage was contracted after the passing of the edict: Aaron was three years old when Moses was born, and we may easily conjecture that he was brought up openly and securely, but there is no doubt that the cruelty was greatest at its commencement; therefore, if they were children of the same mother, there is no other explanation except to say that by the figure called a relating of things out of order he now tells what had happened before. Mention is made only of Moses because it then first began to be criminal to breed up male infants, Calvin says; and the Hebrews use the word for going or departing to signify the undertaking of any serious or momentous matter, or when they put any proposal into operation. Nor is it superfluous for Moses to say that his father married a wife of his own tribe, Calvin adds, because this double tie of kindred should have confirmed them in their attempt to preserve their offspring; but soon afterwards we shall see how timidly they acted, for they hide the child for a short time, rather from the transient impulse of love than from firm affection. When three months had elapsed and that impulse had passed away, they almost abandon the child in order to escape from danger, Calvin says: although the mother would probably have come next day to give him the breast if he had passed the night there, yet she had exposed him as an outcast to innumerable risks, and by this example we perceive what terror had taken possession of every mind, when a man and his wife, united by close natural relationship, prefer exposing their common offspring, whose beauty moved them to pity, to peril of wild beasts, of the atmosphere, of the water and of every kind, rather than that they should perish with him. On this point different opinions are maintained, Calvin allows, whether it would have been better to discharge themselves of the care of their child or to await whatever danger attended his secret preservation; and he confesses that while it is difficult in such perplexities to come to a right conclusion, so also our conclusions are apt to be variously judged, yet he affirms that the timidity of the parents of Moses, by which they were induced to forget their duty, cannot advisedly be excused. We see that God has implanted even in wild and brute beasts so great instinctive anxiety for the protection and cherishing of their young that the dam often despises her own life in their defence, Calvin says: wherefore it is the more base that men, created in the divine image, should be driven by fear to such a pitch of inhumanity as to desert the children who are entrusted to their fidelity and protection. The reply of those who assert that there was no better course in their desperate circumstances than to repose on the providence of God has something in it but is not complete, Calvin says: it is the chief consolation of believers to cast their cares on the bosom of God, provided that in the meantime they perform their own duties, overpass not the bounds of their vocation and turn not away from the path set before them, but it is a perversion to make the providence of God an excuse for negligence and sloth, and the parents of Moses ought rather to have looked forward with hope that God would be the safeguard of themselves and their child. His mother made the ark with great pains and daubed it, Calvin asks, but for what purpose, and was it not to bury her child in it: he allows that she always seemed anxious for him, yet in such a way that her proceedings would have been ridiculous and ineffectual unless God had unexpectedly appeared from heaven as the author of their preservation, of which she herself despaired. On the child's beauty Calvin says there is no doubt that God had adorned him with it in order the more to influence his parents to preserve him, as it sometimes happens that when God sees his people slow in the performance of their duty he spurs on their inactivity by allurements; although it appears from the testimony of the Apostle that this was not their only motive to have pity on him, but that it was the prop of their weak faith, since he tells us that by faith Moses was hid three months of his parents. If any object that faith and regard for beauty are things not only very different but almost contrary to each other, Calvin replies that by the wonderful compassion of God it comes to pass that the very impediment which might darken faith becomes its assistant, though it ought indeed to rest upon the promises alone: therefore, if faith had shone purely and brightly in their hearts they would have cared nothing for his beauty, while on the other hand, unless the promise had had its power, nay, unless it had occupied the first place, there was no such efficacy in the goodliness of his appearance as would have led them willingly to hazard their lives. We conclude then, Calvin says, that since they had good hopes of the deliverance promised to them, their courage was increased by the additional motive of his beauty, and that they were so attracted to pity that all obstacles were overcome; thus does God ordinarily work, leading his people in their darkness like the blind when they are wavering through ignorance and weakness of heart. In fine, the love which his beauty awakened was so far from being a part of faith that it deservedly detracts from its praise, Calvin concludes, but God, who in his wonderful wisdom makes all things work for the good of his chosen ones, sustained and strengthened their tottering faith by this support. It is probable that the watcher was Miriam, Calvin says, and by the fact of her standing to watch what became of him it appears that his parents had some hope remaining, though it was but small, for it is scarcely doubtful that whatever Egyptian had come that way would have been his executioner, as well from the command of the king as from the general hatred of the nation against the Hebrews; it seems then that Miriam was set by her parents to watch rather to witness her brother's murder than to provide for the safety of the child. But since we have just seen that in the darkness of sorrow and despair some sparks of faith still survived, Calvin says, the mother, exposing her little one on the river's side, did not abandon all care of him but desired to commend him to the mercy of any passer-by, and therefore stationed her daughter afar off to act as circumstances arose; this determination, however, as is often the case in times of perplexity and trouble, was vain, though God miraculously stretched forth his hand for the child's preservation. There can be no question but that his secret providence brought the king's daughter to the river, Calvin says, who had the courage to take up the child and to have it nursed, and that he too influenced her mind to the kind act of saving its life, and in a word that he controlled the whole matter; indeed all pious persons will confess that he was the author of her great and uninquisitive kindness in not taking more pains to learn who were the child's parents, and why a nurse offered herself so immediately, which circumstance might have naturally awakened suspicion. Thus it did not happen without many miracles that the child escaped safely from the ark, Calvin says: scoffers would say that all occurred accidentally, because perverse delusion has possession of their minds so that they are blind to the manifest works of God and think that the human race is governed by mere chance; but we must hold fast to the principle that whilst God rules all men by his providence, he honours his elect with his peculiar care and is watchful for their deliverance and support. To ascribe to fortune such a harmonious combination of various and manifold means is no less absurd than to imagine with Epicurus that the world was created by the fortuitous conjunction of atoms, Calvin says: assuredly he drew out Moses, who was to be the future redeemer of his people, as from the grave, in order that he might prove that the beginning of the safety of his Church was like a creation out of nothing.

Matthew Henry says Moses was a Levite both by father and mother, and that Jacob left Levi under marks of disgrace, and yet soon after Moses appears a descendant from him, that he might typify Christ, who came in the likeness of sinful flesh and was made a curse for us; this tribe began to be distinguished from the rest by the birth of Moses, as afterwards it became remarkable in many other instances. It seems to have been just at the time of his birth that the cruel law was made for the murder of all the male children of the Hebrews, Henry says, and many no doubt perished by the execution of it: the parents of Moses had Miriam and Aaron, both older than he, born to them before this edict came out, and had nursed them without that peril, but those that begin the world in peace know not what troubles they may meet with before they have got through it. Probably the mother of Moses was full of anxiety in the expectation of his birth now that this edict was in force, Henry says, and was ready to say, blessed are the barren that never bore, since it were better so than to bring forth children to the murderer; yet this child proves the glory of his father's house, and thus that which is most our fear often proves in the issue most our joy. Observe the beauty of providence, Henry says: just at the time when Pharaoh's cruelty rose to this height the deliverer was born, though he did not appear for many years after, and when men are projecting the church's ruin God is preparing for its salvation. Moses, who was afterwards to bring Israel out of this house of bondage, was himself in danger of falling a sacrifice to the fury of the oppressor, Henry observes, God so ordering it that, being afterwards told of this, he might be the more animated with a holy zeal for the deliverance of his brethren out of the hands of such bloody men. His parents observed him to be a goodly child, more than ordinarily beautiful, Henry says, for he was fair to God, and they fancied he had a lustre in his countenance that was something more than human and was a specimen of the shining of his face afterwards: God sometimes gives early earnests of his gifts and manifests himself betimes in those for whom and by whom he designs to do great things, as he put an early strength into Samson, an early forwardness into Samuel, wrought an early deliverance for David, and began betimes with Timothy; therefore they were the more solicitous for his preservation, because they looked upon this as an indication of some kind purpose.

Charles Ellicott says the expression that there went a man is idiomatic and has no special force, and bids us note the extreme simplicity of this announcement, comparing it with the elaborate legends wherewith Oriental religions commonly surrounded the birth of those who were considered their founders, as Thoth, Zoroaster and Orpheus; even the name of the man is here omitted as unimportant, and it is difficult to conceive any one but Moses making such an omission. A daughter of Levi means a woman of the same tribe as himself, a descendant of Levi, Ellicott says, and not a daughter in the literal sense, which the chronology makes impossible. Stephen says that Moses was comely before God, Ellicott notes, and Trogus Pompeius spoke of him as recommended by the beauty of his personal appearance; his infantine goodliness intensified the desire of his mother to save his life, but must not be regarded as the main cause of her anxiety. She hid him three months, that is as long as she could hope to conceal him effectually, Ellicott says, and it must be remembered that Egyptians were mixed up with Israelites in Goshen, and that each Hebrew household would be subjected to espionage from the time of the issue of the edict. An ark of bulrushes is literally a chest of the papyrus plant, Ellicott says, the words used being both of Egyptian origin: teb, teba or tebat is a box or chest in Egyptian and is well Hebraised by tebah, while the papyrus plant was kam in Egyptian, as in modern Coptic, whence probably the Hebrew gome; it was a material frequently used by the Egyptians for boats and even larger vessels. By slime seems to be meant bitumen or mineral pitch, Ellicott says, and by pitch the ordinary vegetable pitch of commerce, mineral pitch, though not a product of Egypt, having been imported into the country from Mesopotamia and largely used for embalming. A rank aquatic vegetation abounds on the Lower Nile and in all the back-waters and marshy tracts connected with it, Ellicott says, and Jochebed placed her child in the flags that the ark might not float away down the river and so be lost to her sight, the word used for flag seeming to be a Hebraised form of a common Egyptian word having this sense. His sister is presumably Miriam, the only sister of Moses mentioned elsewhere, Ellicott says, and to have taken the part which is assigned her in this chapter she must have been a girl of some fourteen or fifteen years of age, and possessed of much quickness and intelligence. Keil and Delitzsch say that at the time when all the Hebrew boys were ordered to be thrown into the Nile there went a man of the house of Levi, the verb contributing to the pictorial character of the account and serving to bring out its importance; according to a later chapter it was Amram, of the Levitical family of Kohath, and he married a daughter, that is a descendant, of Levi, named Jochebed, who bore him a son. From a later chapter we learn that Moses was not the first child of this marriage but his brother Aaron, Keil says, and it is evident that when Moses was born his sister Miriam was by no means a child; both of these had been born before the murderous edict was issued, and they are not mentioned here because the only question in hand was the birth and deliverance of Moses, the future deliverer of Israel. She placed the infant in an ark of bulrushes by the bank of the Nile, hoping that possibly it might be found by some compassionate hand and still be delivered, Keil says; the phrase means a little chest of rushes, and the use of the word for ark is probably intended to call to mind the ark in which Noah was saved, while the papyrus or paper reed was a kind of rush which was very common in ancient Egypt but has almost entirely disappeared, or, as one authority affirms, is nowhere to be found.

Adam Clarke summarises the chapter before expounding it, that Amram and Jochebed marry, that Moses is born and hidden by his mother three months, that he is exposed in an ark of bulrushes on the river Nile and watched by his sister, that he is found by the daughter of Pharaoh, who commits him to the care of his own mother and has him educated as her own son, and that when grown up he is brought to Pharaoh's daughter, who receives him as her own child and calls him Moses. The man was Amram, son of Kohath, son of Levi, Clarke says, and the daughter of Levi was Jochebed, sister to Kohath and consequently both the wife and aunt of her husband Amram, such marriages being at this time lawful though they were afterwards forbidden; but it is possible that daughter of Levi means no more than a descendant of that family, and that probably Amram and Jochebed were only cousins german. As a new law was to be given and a new priesthood formed, Clarke says, God chose a religious family out of which the lawgiver and the high priest were both to spring. This certainly was not her first child, Clarke notes, for Aaron was fourscore and three years old when Moses was but fourscore, and there was a sister, probably Miriam, who was older than either, Miriam and Aaron having no doubt been both born before the decree was passed for the destruction of the Hebrew male children. The text simply says that he was good, Clarke says, which signifies that he was not only a perfect, well-formed child but that he was very beautiful, whence the Septuagint translate the place as seeing him to be beautiful, which Stephen interprets as comely to God, or divinely beautiful; this very circumstance was wisely ordained by the kind providence of God to be one means of his preservation, since scarcely anything interests the heart more than the sight of a lovely babe in distress, his beauty inducing even his parents to double their exertions to save him and being probably the sole motive which led the Egyptian princess to take such particular care of him and to educate him as her own, which in all likelihood she would not have done had he been only an ordinary child. An ark of bulrushes is a small boat or basket made of the Egyptian reed called papyrus, so famous in all antiquity, Clarke says: this plant grows on the banks of the Nile and in marshy grounds, the stalk rising to the height of six or seven cubits above the water, triangular, and terminating in a crown of small filaments resembling hair, which the ancients used to compare to a thyrsus. This reed was of the greatest use to the inhabitants of Egypt, the pith contained in the stalk serving them for food and the woody part to build vessels with, Clarke says, which vessels frequently appear on engraved stones and other monuments of Egyptian antiquity, for which purpose they made it up like rushes into bundles and by tying them together gave their vessels the necessary figure and solidity. Doctor Shaw says that the vessels of bulrushes or papyrus were no other than large fabrics of the same kind with that of Moses, which from the late introduction of planks and stronger materials are now laid aside, Clarke reports; and Pliny takes notice of ships made of papyrus and the equipments of the Nile, and observes elsewhere that of the papyrus itself they construct sailing vessels, while Herodotus and Diodorus have recorded the same fact, and among the poets Lucan writes that the Memphian boat is constructed from the soaking papyrus, the epithet for soaking being particularly remarkable as corresponding with great exactness to the nature of the plant and to its Hebrew name, which signifies to soak or to drink up. She laid it in the flags, Clarke says, not willing to trust it in the stream for fear of a disaster, and probably choosing the place to which the Egyptian princess was accustomed to come. John Wesley says the man went from the place of his abode to another place, and that a daughter means the grand-daughter of Levi. It seems just at the time of his birth that the cruel law was made for the murder of all the male children of the Hebrews, Wesley says, and many no doubt perished by the execution of it, while the parents of Moses had Miriam and Aaron, both elder than he, born to them before that edict came out; probably his mother had little joy of her being with child of him now this edict was in force, yet this child proves the glory of his father's house. Observe the beauty of providence, Wesley says: just when Pharaoh's cruelty rose to this height the deliverer was born; and she hid him three months in some private apartment of their own house, though probably with the hazard of their lives had he been discovered. It is said that the parents of Moses hid him by faith, Wesley notes: some think they had a special revelation that the deliverer should spring from their loins, but however that be, they believed the general promise of Israel's preservation, and in that faith hid their child. God put it into their hearts to put him in an ark of bulrushes by the river side, Wesley concludes, to bring about his own purposes, that Moses might by this means be brought into the hands of Pharaoh's daughter, and that by his deliverance a specimen might be given of the deliverance of God's church.

debates: Whether the parents are to be praised or blamed: Keil, Ellicott, Clarke, Wesley and Gill all read the ark and its placing as careful contrivance, Wesley saying God put it into their hearts and Clarke that she chose the spot the princess frequented; Calvin says instead that the impulse of love passed after three months and they almost abandoned the child, that their timidity cannot advisedly be excused, and that it is baser in men made in God's image than in brute beasts, whose dams despise their own lives for their young

Whether providence excuses them: Calvin refuses the plea that they were resting on God's providence, since it is a perversion to make providence an excuse for negligence and sloth, and asks what the ark was daubed for if not to bury the child; Wesley and Henry both read the same events as providence working through the parents rather than around them

What force the opening verb carries: Ellicott says the expression is idiomatic and has no special force; Keil says it contributes to the pictorial character and brings out the importance of the account; Calvin says the Hebrews use it of undertaking any serious or momentous matter

How the beauty stands to the faith: Calvin holds that faith and regard for beauty are almost contrary, so that the love the child's looks awakened deservedly detracts from the praise of their faith, though God made the impediment an assistant; Clarke and Henry treat the beauty simply as a providential means of preservation, and Ellicott warns only that it must not be taken for the main cause of the mother's anxiety
outliers: Ellicott's argument for authorship from omission, that the extreme simplicity here, beside the elaborate birth legends of Thoth, Zoroaster and Orpheus, and the suppression even of the father's name, is difficult to conceive of anyone but Moses

Clarke's classical apparatus for the papyrus boat, with Doctor Shaw, Pliny twice, Herodotus, Diodorus and Lucan's line on the Memphian boat built of soaking papyrus, the epithet answering to the Hebrew name for the plant

Ellicott's Egyptian etymologies, that both the word for the chest and the word for the reed are of Egyptian origin, and that the mineral pitch was not native but imported from Mesopotamia for embalming
Keil's suggestion that the word for ark is used to call to mind the ark in which Noah was saved
Gill's two chronologies, the rabbinic date of a Wednesday in Adar in the thirty-seventh year after Levi's death, and Bishop Ussher's forty-first year, four generations of the world apart
Calvin's comparison of those who ascribe the rescue to fortune with Epicurus, who imagined the world made by the fortuitous conjunction of atoms

5.pericope_label: Pharaoh’s daughter finds the ark, has compassion, and pays the child’s own mother to nurse him; he becomes her son and is named Moses

schools.summary: John Gill says her name in Josephus is Thermuthis, and by Artapanus, a heathen writer, Merrhis, perhaps from Miriam, and frequently by the Jewish writers Bithia, which is the name of a daughter of another Pharaoh, from whence they seem to have taken it. She came down from the palace of her father, Gill says, the gardens of which might lead to the Nile, for Zoan or Tanis, near which the Arabic writers say the ark was laid, was situated on the banks of the river Nile and was the royal seat of the kings of Egypt; though perhaps the royal seat at this time was either Heliopolis, since Apion testifies that it was a tradition of the Egyptians that Moses was an Heliopolitan, or else Memphis, which was not far from it, for Artapanus says that when he fled, after he had killed the Egyptian, it was from Memphis that he passed over the Nile to go into Arabia. No doubt a bath was there provided for the use of the royal family, Gill adds. The ark was shut or covered over, he notes, though doubtless there were some apertures for respiration. Miriam, observing the ark taken up and the maidens walking upon the bank of the river, and other women perhaps gathering about it to see it, made one among them, and after hearing their discourse about it proposed what follows to Pharaoh's daughter, Gill says; and Jarchi says that Pharaoh's daughter tried several Egyptian women to suckle the child, but it would not suck of them, Josephus saying the same, and it is also in the Talmud, which if true gave Miriam a fair opportunity to offer to do this message for her. Pharaoh's daughter fell in at once with the proposal, Gill says, being no doubt overruled by the providence of God to agree to have such a person called; and the child grew in stature and in strength, thriving under the care of its mother and nurse, through the blessing of God. John Calvin says that here their grief is renewed, when his parents are again obliged to give up Moses and he is torn as it were from their bowels, for on this condition he passed over to the Egyptian nation, not only that he should be alienated from his own race but that he should increase the number of their enemies in his own person. It is scarcely credible that he could be long tolerated in the tyrant's court, and amongst the most cruel enemies of Israel, unless he professed to be a partaker of their hatred, Calvin says: we know of what corrupting influences courts are full, it is well known too how great was the pride of the Egyptians, and experience teaches us how prone even the best natures are to yield to the temptations of pleasure, wherefore we must wonder the more that when Moses was engulfed in these whirlpools he still retained his uprightness and integrity. Certainly the hope of their redemption might seem here again to suffer an eclipse, the course of circumstances being all against it, Calvin says, but thus the providence of God, the more circuitously it appears to flow, shines forth all the more wonderfully in the end, since it never really wanders from its direct object or fails of its effect when its due time is come. Nevertheless God, as with an outstretched hand, drew back his servant to himself and to the body of his Church by suggesting in his name the recollection of his origin, Calvin says: for the king's daughter did not give him this name without the preventing Spirit of God, that Moses might know that he was drawn out of the river when he was about to perish; as often then as he heard his name he must needs remember of what people he sprang, and the power of this stimulus must have been all the greater because the fact was known to everybody. The daughter of the king could by no means have intended this, Calvin says, and would rather have wished the memory of his origin to be lost; but God, who put words in the mouth of Balaam's ass, influenced also the tongue of this woman to bear loud and public testimony to the very thing which she would have preferred to conceal, and although she desired to keep Moses with herself, she became his directress and guide in returning to his own people.

Matthew Henry bids us come see the place where that great man lay when he was a little child, in a bulrush basket by the river's side: had he been left to lie there he must have perished in a little time with hunger, if he had not been sooner washed into the river or devoured by a crocodile, and had he fallen into any other hands than those he did fall into, either they would not or durst not have done otherwise than have thrown him straightway into the river. But Providence brings no less a person thither than Pharaoh's daughter, just at that juncture, Henry says, guides her to the place where this poor forlorn infant lay, and inclines her heart to pity it, which she dares do when none else durst; never did poor child cry so seasonably, so happily, as this did, for the babe wept, which moved the compassion of the princess, as no doubt his beauty did. Those are hard-hearted indeed that have not a tender compassion for helpless infancy, Henry says, and how pathetically does God represent his compassion for the Israelites in general considered in this pitiable state. It is very commendable in persons of quality to take cognizance of the distresses of the meanest, and to be helpful and charitable to them, Henry adds; God's care of us in our infancy ought to be often made mention of by us to his praise, for though we were not thus exposed, which that we were not was God's mercy, yet many were the perils we were surrounded with in our infancy, out of which the Lord delivered us; and God often raises up friends for his people even among their enemies.

Charles Ellicott says the princess coming down to wash herself would be quite in accordance with Egyptian ideas, since women were allowed great liberty in Egypt and moved about much as they pleased, cleanliness was especially regarded, and the Nile water was considered healthy and fructifying; the princess would of course seek a part of the river which was reserved for females, and probably Jochebed knew where she was accustomed to bathe. As a princess she was of course accompanied by a number of female attendants, Ellicott says, even ordinary Egyptian ladies seeming to have been attended at the bath by four or five such persons, though one of them was more especially her waiting-woman, and to her the princess addressed herself. The princess opened the ark herself, perhaps suspecting what was inside, perhaps out of mere curiosity, Ellicott says; the boy wept through hunger, or cold, or perhaps general discomfort, an ark of bulrushes not having been a very pleasant cradle, and the babe's tears moved her to pity while her pity prompted her to save it. She must have shown some sign of her intention, perhaps by taking the child from the ark and fondling it, before Miriam could have ventured to make her suggestion, Ellicott says; and the circumstances spoke for themselves, since no mother would have exposed such a goodly child to so sad a death but one with whom it was a necessity. Miriam had bided her time, Ellicott continues: she had still kept in the background but had approached within hearing distance, and when the princess observed that the babe must be one of the Hebrews' children she was prompt with the rejoinder; if the child was to be nursed at all, if he was to be brought up, a Hebrew nurse would be the fittest. Miriam divines the thought of the princess, or half divines, half anticipates it, and helps to make it take a fixed shape, Ellicott says: she assumes that the child is to be brought up, and for the princess, as her protege at any rate, if not something more. Jochebed must have been waiting near, eagerly expecting, perhaps while concealed from sight watching the result, and ready to appear the moment she was summoned, Ellicott says, since Miriam knew where to find her and brought her quickly to the princess; and the princess adopts Miriam's suggestion, for the child is to be nursed for her and is to be hers, so that she will place it out to nurse and pay the customary wages. Josephus regards the words that the child grew as implying a growth that was strange and abnormal, Ellicott says, but nothing more seems to be intended than nature's ordinary course, the child growing and reaching the time when it was usual in Egypt that children should be weaned; we have no means of determining what this time was, and it may have been the completion of the first year, but more probably it was the completion of the second. Jochebed carried out the terms of her engagement faithfully and gave up her son to the princess at the time agreed upon, Ellicott says; he became her son possibly by a formal act of adoption, but we have at present no evidence that adoption was an Egyptian custom, and perhaps the writer means simply that she brought him up as if he had been her son, gave him a son's education and a son's privileges. The name is in Egyptian probably Mesu, Ellicott says, which is found as a name in the monuments of the nineteenth dynasty and which is common as the latter half of a name, as in Ra-mesu, Aah-mesu and Amen-mesu; in ordinary use this word meant born and son, comparable to the Latin, but it was derived from an Egyptian verb meaning to produce or to draw forth, and the princess justified her imposition of the name by a reference to this etymology, while owing to the existence of a cognate verb in Hebrew it was possible to transfer her explanation into the Hebrew language exactly and literally, though the play upon words cannot be rendered in English. On the education of Moses Ellicott adds that he would be educated like the sons of princesses generally, not like those of priests or of persons destined for the literary life, and that when Stephen says Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians he probably does not mean more than this. It would consist in the first place of orthography and grammar, Ellicott says, Moses being taught to speak the Egyptian language and to write it correctly: he would probably not be taught the hieroglyphic character, the knowledge of which was reserved to the priests, but would be familiarised with the ordinary cursive writing which was the common character for books and even for official documents in his day. Care would be taken to instruct him in the graces of style so far as they were understood at the time, Ellicott continues, and he would be especially practised in epistolary correspondence, which was regarded as one of the most necessary of all gentlemanlike accomplishments; whether his attention would be turned to poetry might perhaps be doubtful, but he would certainly be taught a clear and perspicuous prose style such as was required for official reports. The next branch would be arithmetic and geometry, Ellicott says: the Egyptians had made considerable progress in the former and their calculations ran up to billions, while in the latter they are said to have been exact and minute but not to have pushed their investigations very far, it being sufficient for a youth of the upper classes to be able to keep correct accounts. He would be further instructed in morality, and in the Egyptian views on the subjects of the divine nature, of the relations subsisting between God and man, of a future life and of a judgment to come, Ellicott concludes, Egyptian morality having been for the most part correct so far as it went. Keil and Delitzsch say the exposure of the child at once led the king's daughter to conclude that it was one of the Hebrews' children, and that the fact that she took compassion on the weeping child and, notwithstanding the king's command, took it up and had it brought up, of course without the knowledge of the king, may be accounted for from the love to children which is innate in the female sex, and the superior adroitness of a mother's heart, which co-operated in this case, though without knowing or intending it, in the realization of the divine plan of salvation. Keil quotes Augustine that the divine vengeance was fitting, that the murderer of children should be punished through his own affections and should perish by the provision of his daughter, who had forbidden mothers to bring forth. With the directions to take the child away and suckle it, the king's daughter gave the child to its own mother, who was unknown to her and had been fetched as a nurse, Keil says. When the child had grown large, that is had been weaned, the mother who acted as nurse brought it back to the queen's daughter, who then adopted it as her own son and called it Moses, saying that out of the water she had drawn him, Keil says; and as Pharaoh's daughter gave this name to the child as her adopted son, it must be an Egyptian name, the Greek form of the name also pointing to this, as Josephus affirms. Thermuthis imposed this name upon him from what had happened when he was put into the river, Keil quotes Josephus as saying, for the Egyptians call water Mo and those who are rescued from the water Uses; and the correctness of this statement is confirmed by the Coptic, which is derived from the old Egyptian, though Josephus gives a somewhat different explanation in his book against Apion.

Adam Clarke says Josephus calls her Thermuthis and reports that the ark was borne along by the current, that she sent one who could swim after it, that she was struck with the figure and uncommon beauty of the child, and that she inquired for a nurse, but he having refused the breasts of several and his sister proposing to bring a Hebrew nurse, his own mother was procured; but all this is in Josephus's manner, Clarke says, as well as the long circumstantial dream that he gives to Amram concerning the future greatness of Moses, which cannot be considered in any other light than that of a fable, and not even a cunningly devised one. Whether the daughter of Pharaoh went to bathe in the river through motives of pleasure, health or religion, or whether she bathed at all, the text does not specify, Clarke says: it is merely stated by the sacred writer that she went down to the river to wash, for the word herself is not in the original. Harmer is of opinion that the time referred to was that in which the Nile begins to rise, Clarke reports, and that as the dancing girls in Egypt are accustomed now to plunge themselves into the river at its rising, by which act they testify their gratitude for the inestimable blessing of its inundations, so it might have been formerly, and that Pharaoh's daughter was now coming down to the river on a similar account; but Clarke sees no likelihood in all this. If she washed herself at all it might have been a religious ablution, and yet extended no farther than to the hands and face, Clarke says, for the Hebrew word to wash is repeatedly used in the Pentateuch to signify religious ablutions of different kinds; and Jonathan in his Targum says that God had smitten all Egypt with ulcers, and that the daughter of Pharaoh came to wash in the river in order to find relief, and that as soon as she touched the ark where Moses was her ulcers were healed, which Clarke calls all fable. He believes there was no bathing in the case but simply what the text states, washing, not of her person but of her clothes, which was an employment that even kings' daughters did not think beneath them in those primitive times, Clarke says: Homer represents Nausicaa, daughter of Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians, in company with her maidens, employed at the seaside in washing her own clothes and those of her five brothers, and while thus employed they find Ulysses just driven ashore after having been shipwrecked, utterly helpless, naked and destitute of every necessary of life; the whole scene is so perfectly like that before us that they appear to Clarke to be almost parallels, and he quotes the Greek at length with Cowper's translation. The sight of a beautiful babe in distress could not fail to make the impression here mentioned, Clarke says; it has already been conjectured that the cruel edict of the Egyptian king did not continue long in force, and it will not appear unreasonable to suppose that the circumstance related here might have brought about its abolition, since the daughter of Pharaoh, struck with the distressed state of the Hebrew children from what she had seen in the case of Moses, would probably implore her father to abolish this sanguinary edict. Had not the different circumstances marked here been placed under the superintendence of an especial providence, Clarke says, there is no human probability that they could have had such a happy issue: the parents had done everything to save their child that piety, affection and prudence could dictate, and having done so they left the event to God. By faith, says the apostle, Moses when he was born was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child, and they were not afraid of the king's commandment, Clarke notes: because of the king's commandment they were obliged to make use of the most prudent caution to save the child's life, and their faith in God enabled them to risk their own safety, for they feared God and they had no other fear. From the time of his being brought home by his nurse his education commenced, Clarke says, and he was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, who in the knowledge of nature probably exceeded all the nations then on the face of the earth. The name is from the Hebrew verb signifying to draw out, and Moses is the person drawn out, the word being used in the same sense in the Psalms and in the second book of Samuel, Clarke says: what name he had from his parents we know not, but whatever it might be it was ever after lost in the name given to him by the princess of Egypt; and Abul Farajius says that Thermuthis delivered him to the wise men Janees and Jimbrees to be instructed in wisdom. John Wesley says Providence brings no less a person than Pharaoh's daughter just at that juncture, guides her to the place where this poor infant lay, and inclines her heart to pity it, which she dares do when none else durst; never did poor child cry so seasonably as this did, for the babe wept, which moved her compassion, as no doubt his beauty did. The tradition of the Jews is that Pharaoh's daughter had no child of her own and that she was the only child of her father, Wesley says, so that when he was adopted for her son he stood fair for the crown; however, it is certain he stood fair for the best preferments of the court in due time, and in the meantime had the advantage of the best education, with the help of which he became master of all the lawful learning of the Egyptians. Those whom God designs for great services he finds out ways to qualify them, Wesley says: Moses, by having his education in a court, is the fitter to be a prince and king in Jeshurun; by having his education in a learned court, for such the Egyptian then was, is the fitter to be an historian; and by having his education in the court of Egypt, is the fitter to be employed as an ambassador to that court in God's name. The Jews tell us that his father at his circumcision called him Joachim, but Pharaoh's daughter called him Moses, drawn out of the water, so it signifies in the Egyptian language, Wesley says; the calling of the Jewish lawgiver by an Egyptian name is a happy omen to the Gentile world and gives hopes of that day when it should be said, Blessed be Egypt my people, and his tuition at court was an earnest of the performance of that promise, that kings shall be thy nursing fathers and queens thy nursing mothers.

debates: What the princess came to the river for: Clarke denies there was any bathing, since the word for herself is not in the original, and takes it of washing clothes, an employment kings' daughters did not think beneath them, citing Homer's Nausicaa as an almost exact parallel; Ellicott takes the bathing at face value and defends it from Egyptian custom and the reputation of Nile water; Clarke also rejects Harmer's theory of a ritual plunge at the Nile's rising and the Targum's tale of healed ulcers

Whether the name is Egyptian or Hebrew: Ellicott derives it from the Egyptian Mesu found in nineteenth-dynasty monuments and from a verb meaning to draw forth, the play transferring into Hebrew because a cognate verb exists; Keil insists it must be Egyptian since an Egyptian gave it, and follows Josephus that Mo is water and Uses one rescued from it, noting that Josephus gives another account elsewhere; Clarke keeps it purely Hebrew and admits we do not know what name the parents gave; Wesley reports the tradition that his father called him Joachim

Why the child was not nursed by an Egyptian: Gill and Clarke both report from Josephus, with Jarchi and the Talmud, that he refused the breast of several Egyptian women, which gave Miriam her opening; Ellicott reconstructs it without the legend, holding that the princess must have shown her intention first and that Miriam half divines and half anticipates her thought

Whether the adoption was formal: Ellicott doubts it, since we have as yet no evidence that adoption was an Egyptian custom, and thinks the writer may mean only that she brought him up as a son; Keil says plainly that she adopted him; Wesley reports the tradition that as her only son he stood fair for the crown
outliers: Calvin's reading of the name as an unintended witness, the princess bearing public testimony to the very origin she would have preferred to conceal, as God once put words in the mouth of Balaam's ass
Clarke's judgement on Josephus, that the swimmer sent after the ark and the long circumstantial dream given to Amram are fable, and not even cunningly devised
Keil's quotation of Augustine, that the murderer of children was fitly punished through his own affections and perished by the provision of his daughter

Ellicott's reconstruction of a prince's Egyptian schooling, with the cursive and not the hieroglyphic character, letter-writing as the most necessary gentlemanlike accomplishment, and calculations running up to billions
Clarke's conjecture that the princess, moved by what she saw, may herself have procured the repeal of the edict against the Hebrew children
Wesley's threefold providence, that a court education fitted Moses to be a prince, a learned court to be an historian, and the Egyptian court to be an ambassador to that very court in God's name

11.pericope_label: Moses grown goes out to his brethren, sees an Egyptian smiting a Hebrew, looks about him, kills the Egyptian and hides him in the sand

schools.summary: John Gill says Moses was grown to man's estate, some of the Jewish writers saying he was eighteen and others twenty years of age, but Stephen, who is most to be credited, says he was full forty years of age. He looked this way and that way, that is all around, to observe if there were any within sight who could see what he did, Gill says; which did not arise from any consciousness of any evil he was about to commit, but for his own preservation, lest, if seen, he should be accused to Pharaoh and suffer for it. John Calvin says that now did that faith which the Apostle celebrates begin to show itself, when Moses, despising the pleasures and riches of the Court, chose rather to suffer the reproach of Christ than to be accounted happy apart from companionship with the chosen people. Nor was it only love for his nation but faith in the promises which induced him to undertake this charge, by which he knew that he should incur the hatred of all the Egyptians, Calvin says: although he did not immediately resign his wealth and honourable station and influence and power, this was as it were the preparation for divesting himself of all these deceitful allurements, whence the Apostle says he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. There is certainly no doubt but that he avowed his desire to return to his true and natural kindred from whom he had been separated, Calvin says, for we gather from the context that he did not come to see his brethren only to pity their estate but to bring them some consolation and even to share their lot; nor was the Court so near that he could daily visit them in his ordinary walk, and it is said that he went out the second day. Therefore he privately withdrew himself from the Court, or, having asked permission, preferred to expose himself to enmity rather than not discover his affectionate regard to his people, Calvin says; and he relates that he looked on their burdens or troubles, so that their unjust oppression must have naturally aroused him to give them help, adding another motive, that he saw an Egyptian smiting a Hebrew. It is probable that they were harshly treated by their taskmasters if they were slow in their work, Calvin says, and since they were given over to the will of wicked men, that every one might exercise the same cruelty upon them with impunity. Hence it more evidently appears that Moses came with the design of succouring his unhappy brethren and of relieving and aiding them with his help, Calvin says, since by killing the Egyptian he avenged the injury done indeed to an individual but having a bearing on the whole nation. But although he was inspired by the Holy Spirit with special courage for the performance of this act, Calvin continues, still it was accompanied with an infirmity which shows that he did not undertake without hesitation what he yet knew to be his vocation; for Stephen bears witness that Moses was not impelled by a rash zeal to slay the Egyptian, but because he knew that he was divinely appointed to be the avenger and deliverer of his nation. Still he looked about to see whether any one saw him, and dared not punish the wrongdoer except by a secret blow, Calvin says: thus we perceive that he was not altogether so bold as he should have been, and that he had to strive against his timidity; again, we gather from his hesitation that his faith was weak, so that we must not suppose that it was thus praised by the Apostle because it was absolutely perfect. In the first place then let us conclude that Moses did not rashly have recourse to the sword, Calvin says, but that he was armed by God's command and, conscious of his legitimate vocation, rightly and judiciously assumed that character which God assigned to him; thence it follows that private persons would act improperly, and would be by no means countenanced by his example, if they sought to repress wrong by force and arms. Thus far we should imitate Moses in rendering aid to the suffering and oppressed as far as our means go, and in caring not to incur the ill-will of the wicked when we oppose ourselves to their oppressions, Calvin says, but we must leave it to the judges, who are invested with public authority, to draw the sword of vengeance; if these do not afford their aid to the innocent when they are unjustly treated, all we can do is to murmur, as not even Moses would have been allowed to proceed further unless he had been the appointed avenger and deliverer of the people. As to the fear by which he betrayed his pusillanimity and his present unpreparedness for fulfilling his office, Calvin concludes, let us learn that the obedience of the saints, which is stained by sin, is still sometimes acceptable with God through mercy; and therefore, although the weakness of the flesh is a drawback to us in the performance of our duty, still let us cease not to struggle against it, for our assurance of this ought to have no small effect in animating us, when we are persuaded that there is pardon ready for our hesitation if we do not yield to it.

Matthew Henry says Moses had now passed the first forty years of his life in the court of Pharaoh, preparing himself for business, and now it was time for him to enter upon action; and he boldly owns and espouses the cause of God's people, the best exposition of the words being from an inspired pen in the letter to the Hebrews. By this he expressed his holy contempt of the honours and pleasures of the Egyptian court, Henry says, for he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, since he went out: the temptation was indeed very strong, for he had a fair opportunity to make his fortune and to have been serviceable to Israel too with his interest at court, and he was obliged in gratitude as well as interest to Pharaoh's daughter, and yet he obtained a glorious victory by faith over his temptation, reckoning it much more his honour and advantage to be a son of Abraham than to be the son of Pharaoh's daughter. He also expressed his tender concern for his poor brethren in bondage, with whom, though he might easily have avoided it, he chose to suffer affliction, Henry says: he looked on their burdens as one that not only pitied them but was resolved to venture with them, and if occasion were, to venture for them. He gives a specimen of the great things he was afterwards to do for God and his Israel in two little instances, related particularly by Stephen with design to show how their fathers had always resisted the Holy Ghost, even in Moses himself when he first appeared as their deliverer, wilfully shutting their eyes against this day-break of their enlargement, Henry says; he found himself, no doubt, under a divine direction and impulse in what he did, and knew that he was in an extraordinary manner called of God to do it. Moses was afterwards to be employed in plaguing the Egyptians for the wrongs they had done to God's Israel, Henry concludes, and as a specimen of that he killed the Egyptian who smote the Hebrew, probably one of the Egyptian taskmasters whom he found abusing his Hebrew slave.

Charles Ellicott says notes of time are used with considerable latitude by the sacred writers, and that according to the tradition followed by Stephen Moses was full forty years old when he took the step here indicated; we might have expected him to have come forward sooner, but there may have been difficulties in his so doing. It is remarkable that he does not tell us anything of his life during youth or early manhood, Ellicott says, and later tradition was full of details which, however, are worthless. It is probable that Pharaoh's daughter had never concealed from Moses that he was not her own child but one of the oppressed race, Ellicott says, and she may even have allowed him to hold communication with his family; it is not, however, a mere visit that is here spoken of, but a complete withdrawal from the palace and renunciation of his position at the court, as the letter to the Hebrews says that by faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season. It is the first sign of that strong sympathy and tender affection for his people which characterises him throughout the narrative, Ellicott says, and culminates in the pathetic cry that God should forgive them, and if not, blot him out of his book. Looking on their burdens means that he examined into their condition, watched their treatment and made himself acquainted with it by personal inspection, Ellicott says; and the Egyptian he spied was probably a taskmaster chastising one of the labourers whom he accused of idling, Stephen regarding the act as one of oppression and wrongdoing, as Moses must certainly have viewed it, or he would not have been so moved to indignation as to kill the man. Though not a cruel nation, the Egyptians no doubt, like other slave-drivers, occasionally abused their power and treated the unfortunate labourers with cruelty, Ellicott says. He looked this way and that way to see that no one observed him, Ellicott continues; and on the killing, Jewish commentators gloss over the act or even eulogise it as patriotic and heroical, but it was clearly the deed of a hasty and undisciplined spirit: the offence did not deserve death, and if it had, Moses had neither legal office nor divine call justifying him in making himself an executioner, the result being that by his one wrong act Moses put it out of his power to do anything towards alleviating the sufferings of his brethren for forty years. To the east of the Delta the sand creeps up close to the cultivated grounds, Ellicott says, and there are even patches of it within the Delta itself; Moses naturally remembered that he dug the grave in the sand, where any other writer would probably have said in the ground. Keil and Delitzsch say the education of Moses at the Egyptian court could not extinguish the feeling that he belonged to the people of Israel, and that our history does not inform us how this feeling, which was inherited from his parents and nourished in him when an infant by his mother's milk, was fostered still further after he had been handed over to Pharaoh's daughter, and grew into a firm, decided consciousness of will. All that is related is how this consciousness broke forth at length in the full-grown man, Keil says, in the slaying of the Egyptian who had injured a Hebrew, and in the attempt to reconcile two Hebrew men who were quarrelling; both of these occurred in those days, that is in the time of the Egyptian oppression, when Moses had become great, that is had grown to be a man.

Adam Clarke says Moses was full forty years of age, as Stephen says, when it came into his heart to visit his brethren, that is, he was excited to it by a divine inspiration; and seeing one of them suffer wrong by an Egyptian smiting him, probably one of the taskmasters, he avenged him and slew the Egyptian, supposing that God, who had given him commission, had given also his brethren to understand that they were to be delivered by his hand. Probably the Egyptian killed the Hebrew, Clarke says, and therefore on the precept given to Noah Moses was justified in killing him; and he was authorised so to do by the commission which he had received from God, as all succeeding events amply prove. Previously to the mission of Moses to deliver the Israelites, Clarke reports from Josephus, the Ethiopians having made an irruption into Egypt and subdued a great part of it, a divine oracle advised the Egyptians to employ Moses the Hebrew, on which the king of Egypt made him general of the Egyptian forces; with these he attacked the Ethiopians, defeated and drove them back into their own land, and forced them to take refuge in the city of Saba, where he besieged them. Tharbis, daughter of the Ethiopian king, seeing him, fell desperately in love with him and promised to give up the city to him on condition that he would take her to wife, Clarke continues, to which Moses agreed, and the city was put into the hands of the Egyptians; and Stephen probably alluded to something of this kind when he said Moses was mighty in deeds as well as words. John Wesley says Moses looked on their burdens as one that not only pitied them but was resolved to venture with them and for them. It was probably one of the Egyptian taskmasters whom he found abusing his Hebrew slave, Wesley says, and by special warrant from heaven, which makes not a precedent in ordinary cases, Moses slew the Egyptian and rescued his oppressed brother; and the Jews' tradition is that he did not slay him with any weapon, but, as Peter slew Ananias and Sapphira, with the word of his mouth.

debates: Whether the killing was lawful: Ellicott says the Jewish commentators gloss it over or eulogise it as heroical, but that it was the deed of a hasty and undisciplined spirit, since the offence did not deserve death and Moses had neither legal office nor divine call to be an executioner, and that by this one wrong act he lost forty years of usefulness; Calvin holds on Stephen's authority that Moses knew himself divinely appointed avenger and was armed by God's command; Clarke adds that the Egyptian had probably killed the Hebrew, so that the precept given to Noah justified him; Wesley and Henry say he acted by special warrant from heaven

Whether the act may be imitated: Calvin, having justified Moses, forbids the inference, since private persons are by no means countenanced by his example if they repress wrong by force, the sword of vengeance belonging to the judges, and if these fail the innocent all we can do is murmur; Wesley makes the same reservation in a parenthesis, that the warrant makes no precedent in ordinary cases

What the look this way and that way shows: Ellicott takes it as the caution of a man who knew he was doing wrong; Calvin takes it as evidence that Moses was not so bold as he should have been and that his faith was weak, so that the Apostle's praise must not be read as praise of a perfect act; Gill denies it argued any consciousness of evil and refers it wholly to self-preservation

What weight the silent years carry: Ellicott finds it remarkable that Moses says nothing of his youth and dismisses the later traditions as worthless; Clarke retails Josephus at length on the Ethiopian campaign and the princess Tharbis, and uses it to explain Stephen's calling Moses mighty in deeds
outliers: Ellicott's second argument from an incidental detail, that Moses remembered digging the grave in the sand where any other writer would have said in the ground
Josephus's romance, reported by Clarke, of Tharbis the Ethiopian king's daughter offering to surrender her city if Moses would marry her
The Jewish tradition, reported by Wesley, that Moses used no weapon but slew the Egyptian with the word of his mouth, as Peter slew Ananias
Calvin's concession that the obedience of the saints, though stained by sin, is still sometimes acceptable with God through mercy
Keil's observation that the narrative never explains how the feeling nourished by his mother's milk grew into a settled consciousness of will, but only records its breaking forth
Ellicott's remark that the Egyptians were not a cruel nation, but like other slave-drivers occasionally abused their power

13.pericope_label: Moses returns the second day, parts two striving Hebrews, is rebuffed with a threat, and flees from Pharaoh to Midian, where he sits down by the well

schools.summary: John Gill says the second day means the day following. On the rejoinder, Gill says God had designed Moses for a prince and a judge, and so he appeared to be afterwards; but this man's meaning is that he was not appointed by Pharaoh's order then, and so had nothing to do to interfere in their differences and quarrels, though Moses did not take upon him to act in an authoritative way, but to exhort and persuade them to peace and love, as they were brethren. On Pharaoh's pursuit Gill says he sought to slay Moses both for killing the Egyptian, which by the laws of Egypt was death whether the man were bond or free, and for taking part with the Hebrews against the Egyptians; and knowing him to be a wise and valiant man, Pharaoh might fear he would put himself at the head of the Hebrews and cause a revolt, and if there was anything in his dream that an Hebrew child should be born by whom Egypt would be destroyed, he might call it to mind and fear the time was coming; Gill adds that he might be stirred up by courtiers who doubtless envied the growing interest of Moses in his court. John Calvin says this perseverance shows that Moses was firm and determined in his design of returning to his brethren and abandoning the Court, and that he had advisedly renounced its splendour, its wealth and comforts, although he was by no means ignorant of the miseries to which he exposed himself; wherefore we need not wonder if the Apostle says he chose rather to endure the reproach of Christ than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season. The sad sight of the tyrant's violence was anything but an obstacle to his proceeding, Calvin says, because, being prepared by the hope of future recompense to bear the cross, he was superior to present fear. But he does not assume, as before, the character of a judge, Calvin continues, but performs a duty which the law of charity demands of every one, addressing the men who strove together as a peacemaker and exhorting them both to be reconciled, though he especially blames the wrongdoer; this was not peculiar to Moses but the common duty of all believers, when the innocent are harshly treated, to take their part and as far as possible to interpose, lest the stronger should prevail. It can scarcely be done without exasperating those who are disposed to evil, Calvin says, but nothing ought to allow us to be silent while justice is violated by their forwardness, for in this case silence is a kind of consent; yet Moses reproves moderately and in kind terms, because he does not so much wish to reproach him with the greatness of his fault as to find the means of calming his ferocity. No wonder if the headstrong and wicked man repels angrily this mild admonition, Calvin says, for thus are those who are disposed to injustice accustomed to rage as soon as they are reproved and to drive away good advisers with contumely; and certainly it is an uncommon virtue to acknowledge our faults and patiently to submit to correction, for in proportion to a man's evil disposition is his rage under admonition, wherefore whoever undertakes to restrain the wicked must expect to meet with these indignities. We may understand from the petulance of this individual how perverse were the minds of the whole nation, Calvin says, on which account Stephen says that Moses was refused by his own nation and accuses them all of ingratitude; but, without being too hard on this people, we learn from this example how rude is the nature of those whom God has not tamed, for their perverseness as firmly repels correction as an anvil repels the blow of a hammer. When they are so stubborn that though ten times reproved they are still hardened, no wonder if God deals with them more roughly, Calvin says; lest we should experience this, let us submit to his rod in time, and since this is not given to all, let us entreat him to make us truly teachable, for what shall we gain by kicking against the pricks? A kind of brutal fierceness accompanies this perverseness, Calvin adds: the vile and abject slave asks Moses who made him a judge over the Hebrews, as if he and all his race were not exposed to universal contumely; if the lowest of the Egyptian rabble had struck him a blow he would not have dared to murmur, yet he rages as imperiously against this mild admonition as if he were free from all subjection. What follows is even worse, Calvin says, for he ought to have received Moses as if he had been an angel of God on account of such a proof of his zeal and piety, but, turning the benefit into an accusation, he not only hatefully taunts him with what it would have been just to praise but even threatens him; meantime we cannot doubt but that the holy man must have been racked by a sore temptation when he finds such barbarity in his nation, for he knew that the Egyptians would have been his professed enemies if the matter had got abroad, but he never could have expected such an unworthy return from his brethren, whose misery he desired to relieve, and therefore it was a proof of incredible strength of purpose to surmount such an obstacle. On the flight Calvin says Moses acknowledges his fear, though it was not sufficient to withdraw him from the work to which he was called; his zeal was mingled with infirmity but yet prevailed, so that he performed the duty entrusted to him manfully yet at the same time timidly. But this is another proof of his firmness, that he is not ashamed of what he had done so as to endeavour to appease the king, but betakes himself to exile, Calvin says; nor is he so alarmed in this critical time as to sink down in helplessness or despair, but he departs into the land of Midian and prefers wandering in the Desert to a reconciliation with the enemies of the chosen people. Although God appears by this circuitous course to decline from his purpose of delivering them, yet he marvellously carries on His work, Calvin says: Moses was certainly not yet ripe for the arduous contests which awaited him, and, having been brought up delicately and luxuriously in the Court, he was not yet accustomed to the great and continual anxieties of which the sequel will show him the conqueror; therefore God in a manner withdrew him, that he might gradually render him fit and equal to undertake so difficult a task, for the experience of forty years in such a laborious and ascetic mode of life did not a little avail to prepare him for enduring any hardships, so that the Desert may well be called the school in which he was taught until he was invited to his more difficult charge. As to his sitting down by a well, Calvin interprets it that he sat down there to rest from his fatigue about sunset, that he might ask for hospitality from the people who he hoped would come at eventide to draw water; and from this unprosperous beginning he might conjecture what an uncomfortable reception he had to expect.

Charles Ellicott says the second day means the next day, and that the Hebrew for him that did the wrong is simply the wicked one, our version following the Septuagint. He compares the report in Acts, where the words of Moses are given somewhat differently as an appeal to the men as brethren, and says that in either case there was no offensive assumption of authority, but the wrongdoer took offence nevertheless. On the rejoinder Ellicott says that as the reputed son of a princess Moses would be in some sort a prince, but no one had given him jurisdiction over the Hebrews; he had not really interfered as one who claimed authority, but as any man of position and education naturally interferes to stop a quarrel. Here is the sting of the rejoinder, Ellicott says: here was the assumption of authority, not in the interposition of to-day but in the blow of yesterday; that fatal error laid Moses open to attack and deprived him of the influence as a peacemaker which he might otherwise have exercised over his countrymen. We are not told how the thing came to be known, Ellicott says; murder will out, says the English proverb, and perhaps, though Moses thought himself unnoticed, some Egyptian had seen the deed, or perhaps the man whom he had avenged had told the tale. That Pharaoh sought to slay Moses was natural, Ellicott says: the administration of justice was one of the chief duties of the royal office, and the crime committed by Moses was one to be punished by death, there being nothing to reduce it from murder to manslaughter; and the motives which extenuate it in the eyes of moderns, patriotic zeal and hatred of oppression, would not have commanded the sympathies of a Pharaoh. Moses fled, or rather had fled, Ellicott says, for he would fly as soon as he found his act was known, fleeing at the saying of the Israelite, so that when Pharaoh sought for him he was gone. Dwelt in the land of Midian means that he was led to make Midian his home, Ellicott says, and the Midian of this book seems to be the south-eastern portion of the Sinaitic peninsula, not the opposite Arabian coast where were the main settlements of the nation. Sat down by a well should be rather the well, Ellicott concludes: there must have been one principal well in these parts, copious and so generally resorted to, and Moses fixed his temporary abode in its neighbourhood.

Adam Clarke says it is strange that in the very place where they were suffering a heavy persecution because they were Hebrews, the very persons themselves who suffered it should be found persecuting each other; it has often been seen that in those times in which the ungodly oppressed the Church of Christ, its own members have been separated from each other by disputes concerning comparatively unessential points of doctrine and discipline, in consequence of which both they and the truth have become an easy prey to those whose desire was to waste the heritage of the Lord. Clarke adds that the Targum of Jonathan says the two persons who strove were Dathan and Abiram. On Moses fearing, Clarke says he saw that the Israelites were not as yet prepared to leave their bondage, and that though God had called him to be their leader yet his providence had not yet sufficiently opened the way; and had he stayed in Egypt he must have endangered his life, so that prudence dictated an escape for the present to the land of Midian. Clarke then raises the difficulty: how can Moses fleeing from the face of Pharaoh be reconciled with the word that by faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king? Very easily, Clarke answers: the apostle speaks not of this forsaking of Egypt but of his and the Israelites' final departure from it, and of the bold and courageous manner in which Moses treated Pharaoh and the Egyptians, disregarding his threatenings and the multitudes of them that pursued after the people whom, in the name and strength of God, he led in the face of their enemies out of Egypt. The land of Midian is a country generally supposed to have been in Arabia Petraea, on the eastern coast of the Red Sea not far from Mount Sinai, Clarke says, and the place is still called by the Arabs the land of Midian or the land of Jethro, while Abul Farajius calls it the land of the Arabs. It is supposed that the Midianites derived their origin from Midian, the fourth son of Abraham by Keturah, the line running Abraham, Midian, Raguel, Jethro, Clarke says; but Calmet contends that if Jethro had been of the family of Abraham, either by Jokshan or Midian, Aaron and Miriam could not have reproached Moses with marrying a Cushite, Zipporah the daughter of Reuel, and he therefore thinks that the Midianites were of the progeny of Cush the son of Ham. John Wesley says the man challenges his authority in asking who made him a prince: a man needs no great authority for giving a friendly reproof, it is an act of kindness, yet this man needs will interpret it an act of dominion and represents his reprover as imperious and assuming. Thus, when people are sick of good discourse or a seasonable admonition, they will call it preaching, as if a man could not speak a word for God and against sin but he took too much upon him, Wesley says; yet Moses was indeed a prince and a judge, and knew it, and thought the Hebrews would have understood it, but they stood in their own light and thrust him away. See what base constructions malice puts upon the best words and actions, Wesley says: Moses, for reproving him, is presently charged with a design to kill him. On the flight Wesley says God ordered this for wise ends, for things were not yet ripe for Israel's deliverance: the measure of Egypt's iniquity was not yet full, the Hebrews were not sufficiently humbled, nor were they yet increased to such a multitude as God designed, and Moses is to be farther fitted for the service and therefore is directed to withdraw for the present till the set time to favour Israel come. God guided Moses to Midian because the Midianites were of the seed of Abraham and retained the worship of the true God, Wesley says, so that he might have not only a safe but a comfortable settlement among them; and through this country he was afterwards to lead Israel, which, that he might do the better, he now had opportunity of acquainting himself with it. Hither he came and sat down by a well, tired and thoughtful, waiting to see which way Providence would direct him, Wesley concludes: it was a great change with him, since he was but the other day at ease in Pharaoh's court.

debates: Where the offence in the rejoinder lay: Ellicott says the sting is not in the day's interposition, which was no claim of authority at all, but in the previous day's blow, and that this fatal error laid Moses open to attack and cost him his influence as a peacemaker; Wesley and Gill locate the fault wholly in the hearer, Wesley saying a friendly reproof needs no authority and is merely being called dominion, Gill saying Moses never acted authoritatively but only persuaded them as brethren

Whether Moses's flight contradicts the praise of his faith: Clarke raises the difficulty from the word that by faith he forsook Egypt not fearing the wrath of the king, and answers that the apostle speaks of the final Exodus and not of this flight; Calvin instead concedes the fear, saying his zeal was mingled with infirmity yet prevailed, and finds the firmness in his refusing to appease the king and choosing exile

Whose punishment the flight escaped: Ellicott says the crime was murder with nothing to reduce it to manslaughter, and that a Pharaoh would not have felt the modern extenuations of patriotic zeal; Gill makes the pursuit political as much as judicial, adding that Pharaoh feared a wise and valiant man might head a revolt and that courtiers envious of his standing may have stirred him up

Whether the Midianites descended from Abraham: Clarke reports the usual genealogy from Abraham by Keturah through Midian to Raguel and Jethro, and Wesley builds on it, saying God guided Moses there because the Midianites were of Abraham's seed and retained the worship of the true God; but Clarke also reports Calmet's objection that Aaron and Miriam could not then have reproached Moses with marrying a Cushite, and Calmet's conclusion that the Midianites came of Cush the son of Ham
outliers: Clarke's application of the quarrel to church history, that the persecuted Church has repeatedly divided over comparatively unessential points of doctrine and discipline and so become easy prey
The Targum of Jonathan's identification, reported by Clarke, of the two striving Hebrews as Dathan and Abiram
Calvin's anvil, that the perverseness of an untamed nature repels correction as firmly as an anvil repels the blow of a hammer
Calvin's reading of the wilderness as pedagogy, that the Desert may well be called the school in which Moses was taught for forty years until he was invited to his more difficult charge
Ellicott's insistence on the article, that Moses sat down not by a well but by the well, one principal copious well generally resorted to
Wesley's practical note that Moses would afterwards lead Israel through Midian, and now had opportunity of acquainting himself with the country
themes: the cost of the earlier blow

16.pericope_label: Moses at the well of Midian defends the seven daughters of Reuel from the shepherds, is welcomed into the priest of Midian house, marries Zipporah and names his son Gershom

schools.summary: John Gill says the priest of Midian, being a descendant of Abraham, might have retained the knowledge of the true God and might be a priest of his, as Melchizedek was, or otherwise it may be thought improbable that Moses would have married his daughter; and so Aben Ezra says he was a priest of God, though the word is sometimes used of a prince, ruler and governor, and is so rendered here by the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan, while Artapanus, an heathen writer, expressly calls him a prince of those places, that is, of Arabia. He might be both prince and priest, as Melchizedek was, and as has been the usage of many countries, Gill says.
