The shepherds who came and drove them away, Gill says, were shepherds of some neighbouring princes or great men, who were so rude and slothful, and to save themselves a little trouble of drawing water, brought up their flocks to drink of the water those virgins had drawn, and to do this forced them and their flocks away. On Reuel, Gill notes the Septuagint's Ragouel and Artapanus's use of the same, and that the Targum of Jonathan has it their father's father, and so Aben Ezra says he was, and is the sense of others, but it does not follow from thence. The daughters said an Egyptian delivered us, Gill says: a man who by his habit and by his speech appeared to them to be an Egyptian, and upon their inquiry he might tell them so, being born in Egypt, though of Hebrew parents. By the account Reuel's daughters gave of Moses, of his courage and humanity, he was very desirous of seeing him, Gill says. Moses was content to dwell with the man after he had been called and brought into the house and had had some refreshment, and after some conversation and perhaps some days' stay, Gill says: Reuel, having observed his disposition and behaviour and being delighted therewith, proposed to him to take up his residence with him, with which motion Moses was well pleased and accepted of it. Gershom signifies a desolate stranger, Gill says, partly on his own account, he being in a foreign country, a stranger and sojourner, but not by way of complaint, rather of thankfulness to God for providing so well for him in it; and partly on his son's account, that when he came to years of maturity he might learn, and in which Moses no doubt instructed him, that he was not to look upon Midian as his proper country, but that he was to be heir of the land of Canaan, of which he might be reminded by his name. John Calvin says the profane would attribute this meeting to good fortune, whereas God affords us in it a striking picture of his providence, in thus with an outstretched hand directing the steps of his servant; those damsels were in the habit of coming daily to the well, and Moses sat down to ask for hospitality at the waterside, whither in a dry country the inhabitants were likely to flock in the evening. But it was by no means due to chance that he came so opportunely to render assistance to the damsels, and that Jethro so hospitably invited him, Calvin says, but God was the guide of his wandering servant's way, not only to obtain for him a resting-place for a day but a comfortable habitation even to the close of his exile; for Jethro, whose title shows that he was of some dignity amongst his people, not only engaged his services but chose him for his son-in-law, and although the occupation of a shepherd was a humble one, yet there was no little consolation in this high connection. On the word rendered priest, Calvin says the verb does not occur in Hebrew in its primary conjugation but is found in Arabic, where it signifies to draw nigh, so that the noun means in strictness one who draws nigh, and in usage a priest who draws nigh to God, a prince who draws nigh to the sovereign, or sometimes the sovereign's guards, ministers or near kinsmen. The Chaldee paraphrast badly translates it Prince, Calvin says, because it does not accord with the fact that the shepherds of the country were at variance with his daughters; nor is it more probable that a rich and chief man would have been without servants, so as to be obliged to expose his daughters daily to the insults and quarrels of the shepherds; he thinks, then, that he was a priest, which is the opinion most generally received. But the question is whether he worshipped false gods or the one true God, Calvin says, and certainly many probable reasons lead us to conclude that he did not sacrifice to idols, because Moses could scarcely have been persuaded, not merely to live in a house which was defiled by foul unrighteousness, but even to marry into it; besides, many indications of piety will appear hereafter in the language of Jethro. Although, as almost the whole world had then fallen into many corrupt practices, it seems likely that his priesthood was in some measure corrupted, Calvin says: in the time of Abraham, Melchizedek was the only priest of the living God, and Abraham himself was extricated from a deep abyss of idolatry into which his family was plunged, so that it was hardly possible that the Midianites should have retained the pure worship, and indeed it is plain from other passages that they were joined to idols. After duly weighing all these points, nothing occurs to Calvin as more probable than that under the priesthood of Jethro the true God was worshipped, according as tradition had revealed him, but not purely, because religion was at that time everywhere contaminated by diverse superstitions; but there is some difference between idolatry and the impure worship of God, corrupted in some respects. I say, then, that they were worshippers of the true God, Calvin concludes, because they had not entirely departed from the principles of his religion, although they had contracted some defilement from the stinking puddles of error which had gradually crept in. On the names, Calvin holds it quite evident that Moses in the next chapter speaks of the same person under another name, and that it would not agree with the mention of his marriage that the name of the father should be altogether omitted; it will appear probable, he says, that Reuel was the grandfather, Jethro the father, and Hobab the brother, of Zipporah, so that after forty years Reuel is no more spoken of except to notice descent from him. Calvin adds that it would not have been kind to press a man bowed down by age to accompany Moses on his long journey, for if Jethro was older than Moses he was scarcely less than ninety, and what sense would there have been in promising a decrepit old man the reward of his labour after they should reach the land of Canaan; the whole controversy is put an end to in one word, because Moses writes that Jethro returned home but that Hobab was persuaded to remain, nothing being more probable than that the old man, unequal to bear the fatigue of a long journey, returned straight home, having left his son behind with Moses to be to him instead of eyes and to guide them on their way. Calvin does not think any blame attaches to the daughters for not offering hospitality to Moses, because young women should be modest, and it would have been an act of too great forwardness to invite an unknown foreigner without acquainting their father; but God inspires the heart of their father with gratitude, so that he desires him to be sent for. There was need of some alleviation for his manifold cares and sorrows, Calvin says, since it was a hard trial which would have altogether overwhelmed him in despair unless the holy man had been supported in enduring his forty years' exile; we may easily conjecture from our own feelings how great must have been the weariness of so tedious a delay, especially when he saw that the flower of his age was past and that his strength was failing, so that he would be afterwards but little fitted for activity, and it was therefore difficult for him to be intent on that vocation, which might seem to be obsolete and abrogated in this period of forty years. Wherefore God's grace is more astonishing, Calvin says, which kept him peaceful and calm in the midst of so many cares, so that in expectation of the unknown time he should be content with his mean and humble lot and stand in daily preparation to perform the part of a deliverer. On the word used of Reuel's consent, Calvin reports that the Jews themselves are not agreed, many thinking that it merely expresses consent and others taking it to mean to swear; and perhaps Jethro was unwilling to give his daughter to an unknown guest unless he bound himself by an oath to live there, as otherwise it might be feared that Moses might take away his wife elsewhere, so that the marriage-vow was a promise to remain, whence we see the integrity of that age, that the sanction of an oath, through reverence to the name of God, was so strong that both were contented with this bond. On Gershom, Calvin says he does not approve of their view who think this was a name of congratulation to alleviate the pain of banishment, but rather imagines that Moses gave this name to his son, as well to remind himself as his father-in-law and his wife, that he sought a country elsewhere and that there he was but a sojourner. Nor is there any objection in his promise to his father-in-law to remain, Calvin says, because he did not so bind himself as to shake off or break the yoke of his divine vocation; it was only a provision that Moses should not lightly forsake the home where he was so kindly welcomed. It is not credible that he was silent as to the cause of his exile, Calvin adds, in the first place to avert the suspicion of wrong-doing and in witness of his innocence, and secondly that he might proclaim the peculiar favour with which God had honoured the people of Israel; wherefore, in the name of his son, he would set before himself an unceasing memorial by which he might be kept alive to the hope of redemption, for he declares that land, in which he had found apparently a peaceful resting-place and a pleasant home, to be strange to him. Nor does he compare Midian with Egypt, Calvin concludes, for he was but a sojourner in either land, but wherever he may dwell he declares himself a stranger until he should obtain the inheritance which God has promised; in fine, we see that he sought for a means of cherishing and at the same time of testifying his faith, when he professed that he was a sojourner in a foreign land.

Matthew Henry says Moses here gains a settlement in Midian, just as his father Jacob had gained one in Syria, and both these instances should encourage us to trust Providence and to follow it; events that seem inconsiderable and purely accidental afterwards appear to have been designed by the wisdom of God for very good purposes and of great consequence to his people, and a casual transient occurrence has sometimes occasioned the greatest and happiest turns of a man's life. Concerning the seven daughters of Reuel, Henry says they were humble and very industrious, according as the employment of the country was, and drew water for their father's flock: if their father was a prince, it teaches us that even those who are honourably born and are of quality and distinction in their country should yet apply themselves to some useful business, and what their hand finds to do do it with all their might, for idleness can be no one's honour; and if their father was a priest, it teaches us that ministers' children should in a special manner be examples of humility and industry. They were modest, Henry says, and would not ask this strange Egyptian to come home with them, though handsome and a great courtier, till their father sent for him; modesty is the ornament of woman. Moses was taken for an Egyptian, and strangers must be content to be the subjects of mistake, Henry says; but it is observable how ready he was to help Reuel's daughters to water their flocks, for though bred in learning and at court he knew how to turn his hand to such an office when there was occasion, nor had he learned of the Egyptians to despise shepherds. Those that have had a liberal education should not be strangers to servile work, Henry says, because they know not what necessity Providence may put them in of working for themselves, or what opportunity Providence may give them of being serviceable to others. These young women met with some opposition in their employment, more than they and their servants could conquer, Henry says, the shepherds of some neighbouring prince, as some think, or some idle fellows that called themselves shepherds, driving away their flocks; but Moses, though melancholy and in distress, stood up and helped them, not only to get clear of the shepherds but, when that was done, to water the flocks. This he did not only in complaisance to the daughters of Reuel, Henry says, but because wherever he was, as occasion offered itself, he loved to be doing justice and appearing in the defence of such as he saw injured, which every man ought to do as far as it is in the power of his hand to do it, and he loved to be doing good; wherever the Providence of God casts us we should desire and endeavour to be useful, and when we cannot do the good we would we must be ready to do the good we can, and he that is faithful in a little shall be entrusted with more. Henry observes how well he was paid for his serviceableness, for when the young women acquainted their father with the kindnesses they had received from this stranger he sent to invite him to his house and made much of him; thus God will recompense the kindnesses which are at any time shown to his children, and they shall in no wise lose their reward. Moses soon recommended himself to the esteem and good affection of this prince of Midian, Henry says, who took him into his house and in process of time married one of his daughters to him, by whom he had a son whom he called Gershom, a stranger there, that if ever God should give him a home of his own he might keep in remembrance the land in which he had been a stranger. This settlement of Moses in Midian was designed by Providence to shelter him for the present, Henry says: God will find hiding-places for his people in the day of their distress, nay, he will himself be to them a little sanctuary, and will secure them either under heaven or in heaven. But it was also designed to prepare him for the great services he was further designed for, Henry says: his manner of life in Midian, where he kept the flock of his father-in-law, having none of his own to keep, would be of use to inure him to hardship and poverty, that he might learn how to want as well as how to abound, for those whom God intends to exalt he first humbles; and to inure him to contemplation and devotion. Egypt accomplished him as a scholar, a gentleman, a statesman, a soldier, all which accomplishments would be afterwards of use to him, Henry says, but yet he lacked one thing, in which the court of Egypt could not befriend him: he that was to do all by divine revelation must know, by a long experience, what it was to live a life of communion with God, and in this he would be greatly furthered by the solitude and retirement of a shepherd's life in Midian. By the former he was prepared to rule in Jeshurun, but by the latter he was prepared to converse with God in Mount Horeb, near which mount he had spent much of his time, Henry concludes; and those that know what it is to be alone with God in holy exercises are acquainted with better delights than ever Moses tasted in the court of Pharaoh.

Adam Clarke says the priest of Midian may be rendered priest or prince or both, for the original cohen has both meanings, and that the transaction here very nearly resembles that concerning Jacob and Rachel. On the shepherds driving them away, Clarke says the verb, being in the masculine gender, seems to imply that the shepherds drove away the flocks of Reuel's daughters and not the daughters themselves; the fact seems to be that, as the daughters filled the troughs and brought their flocks to drink, the shepherds drove those away and, profiting by the young women's labour, watered their own cattle, so that Moses resisted this insolence and assisted them to water their flocks, in consequence of which they were enabled to return much sooner than they were wont to do. On Reuel, Clarke says that in Numbers this person is called Raguel but the Hebrew is the same in both places, the reason of the difference being that the ayin is sometimes used merely as a vowel and sometimes as g, ng or gn, occasioned by the difficulty of the sound, which scarcely any European organs can enunciate. As pronounced by the Arabs it strongly resembles the first effort made by the throat in gargling, Clarke says, or as Meninski says, it is like the sound made by a calf in seeking its dam; Raguel is the worst method of pronouncing it, and Re-u-el, the first syllable strongly accented, is nearer to the true sound, a proper uniformity in pronouncing the same word wherever it may occur being greatly to be desired. The person in question appears to have several names, Clarke says: here he is called Reuel, in Numbers Raguel, in the next chapter Jethro, in Judges Hobab, and elsewhere Keni, which we translate Kenite; some suppose that Re-u-el was father to Hobab, who was also called Jethro, and this is the most likely. That he may eat bread means that he may be entertained and receive refreshment to proceed on his journey, Clarke says, bread among the Hebrews being used to signify all kinds of food commonly used for the support of man's life. On Zipporah, Clarke reports that Abul Farajius calls her Saphura the black, daughter of Rewel the Midianite, the son of Dedan, the son of Abraham by his wife Keturah, and that the Targum calls her the granddaughter of Reuel; it appears that Moses obtained Zipporah something in the same way that Jacob obtained Rachel, namely for the performance of certain services, probably keeping of sheep. Gershom literally means a stranger, Clarke says, the reason of which Moses immediately adds, for I have been an alien in a strange land. The Vulgate, the Septuagint as it stands in the Complutensian Polyglot and in several manuscripts, the Syriac, the Coptic and the Arabic add to this verse the words about the second son Eliezer, Clarke says, which are found later in Exodus but are certainly necessary here, for it is very likely that these two sons were born within a short space of each other, since Moses is afterwards said to take his wife and his sons, by which it is plain that he had both Gershom and Eliezer at that time; Houbigant introduces this addition in his Latin version and contends that this is its most proper place, but, notwithstanding the authority of the above versions, the clause is found in no copy, printed or manuscript, of the Hebrew text. John Wesley says Moses stood up and helped them because wherever he was, as occasion offered itself, he loved to be doing justice and appearing in the defence of such as he saw injured; he loved to be doing good, and wherever the Providence of God calls us we should desire and endeavour to be useful, and when we cannot do the good we would we must be ready to do the good we can. Wesley says Reuel or Raguel seems to have been their grandfather, and father of Hobab or Jethro, their immediate father. On Gershom, that is a stranger there, Wesley says this settlement of Moses in Midian was designed by Providence to shelter him for the present, God finding hiding places for his people in the day of their distress, and also to prepare him for the services he was further designed to: his manner of life in Midian, where he kept the flock of his father-in-law, would be of use to inure him to hardship and poverty, and to inure him to contemplation and devotion. Egypt accomplished him for a scholar, a gentleman, a statesman, a soldier, all which accomplishments would be afterwards of use to him, Wesley says, but yet lacketh he one thing, in which the court of Egypt could not befriend him: he that was to do all by divine revelation must know what it was to live a life of communion with God, and in this he would be greatly furthered by the retirement of a shepherd's life in Midian. By the former he was prepared to rule in Jeshurun, but by the latter he was prepared to converse with God in mount Horeb, Wesley concludes; and those that know what it is to be alone with God are acquainted with better delights than ever Moses tasted in the court of Pharaoh.

Charles Ellicott says Reuel may have been both priest and prince, like Melchizedek, but there is no reason to doubt that he is here called priest, since Jethro is afterwards represented as exercising priestly functions. The Midianites, descendants of Abraham by Keturah, worshipped the true God and seem to have been at this time a religious people, Ellicott says; the name Reuel, or Raguel, means friend of God, Jethro's sacrifices were for God, and Aaron and the elders eat bread with him before God. That the daughters came and drew water he compares with Rachel, and adds that according to Oriental ideas there is nothing derogatory in the daughters of a chief so acting. The shepherds were those of the neighbourhood, Ellicott says, and the rule of the desert is that those who come to a well take their turns in the use of the water in the order of their arrival, but these rude shepherds declined to wait for their turn; it appears later, by the question of Reuel how it is that they are come so soon to-day, that this rude and unfair conduct of the shepherds was habitual. Moses is again the champion of the oppressed, Ellicott says, but has learnt wisdom by the past and uses no unnecessary violence: his air and manner intimidated the wrongdoers, and they allowed the maidens' sheep to be watered first. That they called him an Egyptian they concluded from his dress and appearance, perhaps even from his speech, Ellicott says; it would be natural for them to make the mistake and for Moses to remember it, and any other author would probably have said a man, or a stranger. And also drew water enough, Ellicott says: the shepherds had consumed some of the maidens' water before Moses's interference, so that he had to draw more for them, another little trait which speaks for the Mosaic authorship. That he may eat bread shows that Arab hospitality was offended that the stranger had not been invited into the tent to partake of the evening meal, Ellicott says, and the feeling of the modern Bedouin would be the same. Reuel must have been so pleased with the manner and appearance of Moses that he invited him to take service with him, perhaps to share his tent, Ellicott says; Moses consented, and in course of time took to wife Zipporah, one of Reuel's daughters, marriage with the Midianites being allowed even under the Law. It has been conjectured that Reuel might have communicated to Moses traditions, or even documents, concerning their common ancestor Abraham and his family, Ellicott says, but there is nothing to indicate the use of letters at this early date by the Midianites. Gershom is almost certainly from ger, a stranger, and sham, there, Ellicott concludes, so Jerome, who translates it advena ibi, and comparably Josephus and the Septuagint, who write the name Gersam. Keil and Delitzsch say that as Reguel gave a hospitable welcome to Moses, in consequence of his daughters' report of the assistance he had given them in watering their sheep, it pleased Moses to dwell with him, the primary meaning of the verb being simply that he was willing; and that although Moses received Reguel's daughter Zipporah as his wife, probably after a lengthened stay, his life in Midian was still a banishment.

debates: Whether Reuel was priest or prince: Clarke says the word means priest or prince or both; Gill reports the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan and the heathen writer Artapanus all making him a prince, but prefers priest with Aben Ezra and allows he may have been both, as Melchizedek was; Ellicott says there is no reason to doubt he is here called priest, since he afterwards exercises priestly functions; Calvin argues the case from the Arabic root and rejects prince on the practical ground that a rich chief would have had servants and not exposed his daughters daily to the shepherds

How pure the Midianite religion was: Ellicott says flatly that the Midianites worshipped the true God and seem at this time to have been a religious people; Calvin agrees that they had not entirely departed from the principles of his religion, but insists the priesthood was in some measure corrupted, since it is plain from other passages that the Midianites were joined to idols, and settles on a graded verdict, that there is some difference between idolatry and the impure worship of God

How many men the names Reuel, Jethro and Hobab denote: Clarke lists five names and thinks it most likely that Reuel was father to Hobab, who was also called Jethro; Calvin makes three generations, Reuel the grandfather, Jethro the father and Hobab the brother-in-law, and argues from Jethro's great age that he returned home from the desert while Hobab remained; Wesley states the same three-generation scheme in a line; Gill reports the Targum of Jonathan's reading of grandfather and says it does not follow

Whom the shepherds drove away: Clarke argues from the masculine gender of the verb that they drove off the flocks and not the daughters, and watered their own cattle from the troughs the women had filled; Gill and Henry read the drove as including the women themselves, Henry adding that the opposition was more than they and their servants could conquer
outliers: Clarke's phonetic excursus on the ayin, which he says the Arabs sound like the first effort made in gargling, or as Meninski says, like a calf seeking its dam, so that Raguel is the worst way to pronounce the name

Clarke's textual note that the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, Coptic and Arabic all add the birth of Eliezer at this verse, and that Houbigant put it here, though the clause is in no Hebrew copy printed or manuscript

Calvin's suggestion that the word rendered Moses was content may mean he swore, so that Jethro required an oath of residence before giving his daughter, and that the marriage-vow was a promise to remain

Ellicott's conjecture, immediately withdrawn, that Reuel might have given Moses traditions or even documents about their common ancestor Abraham, there being nothing to indicate the use of letters among the Midianites at that date
Clarke's report from Abul Farajius that Zipporah was called Saphura the black, and that Moses obtained her as Jacob obtained Rachel, by the performance of services

Henry's inference from the daughters' work that the honourably born should still apply themselves to useful business, since idleness can be no one's honour, and that ministers' children should be examples of industry

23.pericope_label: The king of Egypt dies, Israel sighs and cries under the bondage, and God hears their groaning, remembers his covenant with the patriarchs, looks on the children of Israel and has respect unto them

schools.summary: John Gill says that according to Eusebius, Orus reigned in Egypt when Moses fled from thence, and that two more reigned after him, Acenchres and Achoris, who both died before the deliverance of the children of Israel; but according to Bishop Usher this was the same king of Egypt under whom Moses was born, and from whose face he fled, who died in the sixty-seventh year of his reign, Moses being now sixty years of age and having been in the land of Midian twenty years, and it was about twenty years after this that he was called from thence to be the deliverer of his people, for things are often put close together in Scripture which were done at a considerable distance. The intention of this notice of the death of the king of Egypt is chiefly to show that it made no alteration in the afflictions of the children of Israel for the better, but rather the worse, Gill says. God heard their groaning, that is, the petitions they put up to him with groans and cries, Gill says. And God looked upon the children of Israel with an eye of pity and compassion, and saw all the hardships they laboured under and all the injuries that were done unto them, Gill says; and God had respect unto them, that is, had a favourable regard to them, or knew them, not only knew the Israelites and loved them and approved of them and owned them as his own, all which words of knowledge sometimes signify, but he knew their sorrows and sufferings, and took notice of what was done to them secretly. John Calvin says the demonstrative pronoun marks the forty years in which God kept his servant in suspense, as if he had forsaken him, and that by adding many he expresses the approaching end of the interval; when, therefore, Moses had reached his eightieth year and had married and grown old in the land of Midian, the intolerable cruelty of their tyrannical masters extorted new sighings and cries from the children of Israel. Not that they began then first to grieve and lament, Calvin says, but because they became more alive to their woes, and their duration made them to be felt more acutely; we know that the hope of a happier issue is soothing to our woes, and the hope that some one more kind would succeed the dead tyrant in some measure softened the misery of the afflicted people, but when the change of kings in no wise lightened their oppression their sorrow was increased and forced them to cry out more loudly than before. Thus Calvin understands the words of Moses, that when the tyrant was dead the children of Israel were not treated more humanely and therefore cried out more vehemently. Although it is not likely, Calvin thinks, that the Pharaoh who had at first afflicted them with burdens and taxes, and had commanded their children to be killed, lived till this time, because in that case he would have reigned more than eighty years, which is not usual; before the birth of Moses the Israelites had already been sorely oppressed for many years, nor had the king proceeded at once to so great an atrocity as to command all the males to be killed, but when he found that his cruel edicts availed nothing he advanced to this extremity. From the birth of Moses until the time here spoken of about eighty years had passed, Calvin says, and hence we may suppose that before their deliverance drew near there had been one or more successive kings. When these various changes of circumstances left the condition of the people unchanged, or even made it worse, extreme necessity drew forth this unwonted lamentation, and despair itself drove them to pray, Calvin says; not that there had been an entire neglect of supplication to God before, but because they looked also in other directions, until all earthly means being entirely cut off they were forcibly drawn to seek in earnest for help from above. From this example we learn that, although the pressure of our tribulations weighs us down with sorrow and pain, yet our prayers are not straightway directed to God, and much is required to stimulate our sluggish hearts, Calvin says; Moses also infers that it was no wonder if God's assistance was not earlier afforded, since the children of Israel were stupified in their misery. Let this example teach us to flee to God at once, in order that he may make haste to bestow his grace, Calvin says, and Moses magnifies the mercy of God by this circumstance, that he took not vengeance on their slowness as it deserved, but graciously inclined to their tardy cries; in fact we may observe in this history what is described in the Psalm, that the most stubborn and hard-hearted in their extremity turn their prayers at length to God, rather from the exceeding greatness of their trouble than from the well-regulated exercise of faith. He says by reason of the bondage, Calvin notes, because it is the attribute of God to succour the oppressed, to deliver the captives and to raise up them that are brought low, and this office he constantly performs. As to what is added, that God remembered his covenant, it is the explanation of the cause why he heard their groaning, Calvin says, namely that he might ratify his gratuitous promise made to Abraham and his descendants; he expressly mentions the three patriarchs because God lodged his covenant with them, that it might continue firm for perpetual generations, and indeed, since God is inclined towards us to help us of his own free mercy, so he offers himself and invites us voluntarily, and therefore confidence in prayer must only be sought for in his promises. How far remembrance is possible with God we must learn from its contrary, Calvin concludes: God is said to forget when he does not really and openly appear and stretch forth his hand to help, therefore when we say he remembers we mark the effect of his aid; and in the same way he is said to behold, and its opposite, to turn his back, because we then know that he beholds us when he actually succours us.

Matthew Henry says that probably the murdering of the Israelites' infants did not continue, this part of their affliction attending only the period immediately connected with the birth of Moses and serving to signalize it; the Egyptians now were content with their increase, finding that Egypt was enriched by their labour, so that they might have them for slaves they cared not how many they were, and on this therefore they were intent, to keep them all at work and make the best hand they could of their labour. When one Pharaoh died another rose up in his place that was governed by the same maxims and was as cruel to Israel as his predecessors, Henry says; if there was sometimes a little relaxation it presently revived again with as much rigour as ever, and probably, as the more Israel were oppressed the more they multiplied, so the more they multiplied the more they were oppressed; sometimes God suffers the rod of the wicked to lie very long and very heavily on the lot of the righteous. If Moses in Midian at any time began to think how much better his condition might have been had he stayed among the courtiers, Henry says, he must of himself think this also, how much worse it would have been if he had had his lot with his brethren: it was a great degradation to him to be keeping sheep in Midian, but better so than making brick in Egypt, and the consideration of our brethren's afflictions would help to reconcile us to our own. Now at last they began to think of God under their troubles, and to return to him from the idols they had served, Henry says; hitherto they had fretted at the instruments of their trouble, but God was not in all their thoughts, and thus hypocrites in heart heap up wrath and cry not when he binds them; but before God unbound them he put it into their hearts to cry unto him, and it is a good sign that God is coming towards us with deliverance when he inclines and enables us to cry to him for it. The name of God is here emphatically prefixed to four different expressions of a kind intention towards them, Henry says. God heard their groaning, that is, he made it to appear that he took notice of their complaints; the groans of the oppressed cry aloud in the ears of the righteous God, to whom vengeance belongs, especially the groans of God's spiritual Israel, for he knows the burdens they groan under and the blessings they groan after, and the blessed Spirit by these groanings makes intercession in them. God remembered his covenant, which he seemed to have forgotten but of which he is ever mindful, Henry says, and God had an eye to this, and not to any merit of theirs, in what he did for them. God looked upon the children of Israel: Moses looked upon them and pitied them, but now God looked upon them and helped them, Henry says. And God had a respect unto them, a favourable respect to them as his own; the frequent repetition of the name of God here intimates that now we are to expect something great, a work worthy of God, Henry says, for his eyes, which run to and fro through the earth, are now fixed upon Israel, to show himself strong, to show himself a God in their behalf. God is ever thus a very present help in trouble, Henry concludes: take courage then, ye who, conscious of guilt and thraldom, are looking to him for deliverance, for God in Christ Jesus is also looking upon you, and a call of love is joined with a promise of the Redeemer.

Adam Clarke says that according to Stephen the death of the Egyptian king happened about forty years after the escape of Moses to Midian, and that the words we translate in process of time signify, and it was in many days from these that the king died. It has already been remarked that Archbishop Usher supposes this king to have been Ramesses Miamun, who was succeeded by his son Amenophis, who was drowned in the Red Sea when pursuing the Israelites, Clarke says, but Abul Farajius says it was Amunfathis, or Amenophis, he who made the cruel edict against the Hebrew children. Some suppose that Moses wrote the book of Job during the time he sojourned in Midian, and also the book of Genesis, Clarke reports. God's covenant is God's engagement, Clarke says: he had promised to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob to give their posterity a land flowing with milk and honey, and they are now under the most oppressive bondage, and this was the most proper time for God to show them his mercy and power in fulfilling his promise; this is all that is meant by God's remembering his covenant, for it was now that he began to give it its effect. God had respect unto them means God knew them, that is, he approved of them, Clarke says, and therefore it is said that their cry came up before God and he heard their groaning; the word to know in the Hebrew Bible, as well as its Greek counterpart in the New Testament, is frequently used in the sense of approving, and because God knew, had respect for and approved of them, therefore he was determined to deliver them. For the word God in the last clause of this verse Houbigant reads upon them, Clarke notes, which is countenanced by the Vulgate, Septuagint, Chaldee, Coptic and Arabic and appears to have been the original reading, the difference in the original consisting in the interchange of two letters; our translators insert unto them in order to make up that sense which this various reading gives without trouble. The farther we proceed in the sacred writings the more the history both of the grace and providence of God opens to our view, Clarke says: he ever cares for his creatures and is mindful of his promise, and the very means made use of to destroy his work are, in his hands, the instruments of its accomplishment. Pharaoh orders the male children of the Hebrews to be thrown into the river, Clarke says; Moses, who was thus exposed, is found by his own daughter, brought up as her own son, and from his Egyptian education becomes much better qualified for the great work to which God had called him, and his being obliged to leave Egypt was undoubtedly a powerful means to wean his heart from a land in which he had at his command all the advantages and luxuries of life. His sojourning also in a strange land, where he was obliged to earn his bread by a very painful employment, fitted him for the perilous journey he was obliged to take in the wilderness, Clarke says; and the bondage of the Israelites was also wisely permitted, that they might with less reluctance leave a country where they had suffered the greatest oppression and indignities, for had they not suffered severely previously to their departure there is much reason to believe that no inducements could have been sufficient to have prevailed on them to leave it. Yet their leaving it was of infinite consequence in the order both of grace and providence, Clarke says, as it was indispensably necessary that they should be a people separated from all the rest of the world, that they might see the promises of God fulfilled under their own eyes. From the example of Pharaoh's daughter and the seven daughters of Jethro we learn that in the days of primitive simplicity, and in this respect the best days, the children, particularly the daughters of persons in the highest ranks in life, were employed in the most laborious offices, Clarke says: kings' daughters performed the office of the laundress to their own families, and the daughters of princes tended and watered the flocks, and we have seen similar instances in the case of Rebekah and Rachel. We cannot be too pointed in calling the attention of modern delicate females, who are not only above serving their own parents and family but even their own selves, Clarke says, the consequence of which is that they have neither vigour nor health, their growth for want of healthy exercise is generally cramped, their natural powers are prematurely developed, and their whole course is rather an apology for living than a state of effective life; many of these live not out half their days, and their offspring, when they have any, is more feeble than themselves, so that the race of man where such preposterous conduct is followed is in a state of gradual deterioration, and parents who wish to fulfil the intention of God and nature will doubtless see it their duty to bring up their children on a different plan. Afflictions, under the direction of God's providence and the influence of his grace, are often the means of leading men to pray to and acknowledge God, who in the time of their prosperity hardened their necks from his fear, Clarke concludes: when the Israelites were sorely oppressed they began to pray, and if the cry of oppression had not been among them probably the cry for mercy had not been heard; though afflictions considered in themselves can neither atone for sin nor improve the moral state of the soul, yet God often uses them as means to bring sinners to himself. John Wesley says the king of Egypt died, and after him one or two more of his sons or successors. Probably the murdering of their infants did not continue, that part of their affliction only attending the birth of Moses, to signalize that, Wesley says; and now they were content with their increase, finding that Egypt was enriched by their labour, so that they might have them for their slaves they cared not how many they were, and on this therefore they were intent, to keep them all at work and make the best hand they could of their labour. When one Pharaoh died another rose up in his place that was as cruel to Israel as his predecessors, Wesley says. Now at last they began to think of God under their troubles, and to return to him from the idols they had served, Wesley says; hitherto they had fretted at the instruments of their trouble, but God was not in all their thoughts, and before God unbound them he put it into their hearts to cry unto him, for it is a sign God is coming towards us with deliverance when he inclines us to cry to him for it. God heard their groaning, that is, he made it to appear that he took notice of their complaints, Wesley says: the groans of the oppressed cry loud in the ears of the righteous God, to whom vengeance belongs, especially the groans of God's children, the burdens they groan under and the blessings they groan after. God remembered his covenant, which he seemed to have forgotten but really is ever mindful of, Wesley says, and God had an eye to this and not to any merit of theirs in what he did for them; God looked upon the children of Israel, for Moses looked upon them and pitied them, but now God looked upon them and helped them. God had respect unto them, a favourable respect to them as his own, Wesley concludes, and the frequent repetition of the name of God intimates that now we are to expect something great, his eyes which run to and fro through the earth being now fixed on Israel, to show himself strong, to show himself a God in their behalf.

Charles Ellicott says that in process of time is in the Hebrew in those many days, and that as Moses was now eighty years old and only forty when he quitted Egypt, the Pharaoh from whom he fled must have reigned above forty years; between the commencement of the eighteenth and the close of the nineteenth dynasty two kings only seem to have reigned so long as this, Thothmes the Third and Rameses the Second, so that our choice of the Pharaoh from whom Moses fled lies between these two. The children of Israel sighed, or groaned, Ellicott says: they had perhaps expected that a new king would initiate a new policy, or at any rate signalise his accession by a remission of burdens, but the new monarch did neither. Exceeding bitter cries always find their way to the ears of God, Ellicott says, and the existing oppression was such that Israel cried to God as they had never cried before, and so moved him to have compassion on them; the miraculous action begun in the next chapter is the result of the cries and groans here mentioned. Keil and Delitzsch say that God heard their crying and remembered his covenant with the fathers, and that God saw the children of Israel and noticed them; this seeing and noticing had regard to the innermost nature of Israel, namely as the chosen seed of Abraham, in Baumgarten's words, and God's notice has all the energy of love and pity. Lyra has aptly explained the verb as behaving after the manner of one who knows, by showing love toward them, Keil says, and Luther has paraphrased it correctly, He accepted them.

Why Israel cried only now: Calvin says they did not then first begin to grieve, but that hope of a kinder successor had softened their misery, and when the new king lightened nothing their sorrow was increased, so that despair itself drove them to pray after they had looked in every other direction; Ellicott says the same as history, that they had expected a new policy or at least a remission of burdens at the accession and got neither; Henry and Wesley make it a return from the idols they had served, since hitherto they had fretted at the instruments of their trouble while God was not in all their thoughts
